q: How many parts are there in traffic book?
e: 4 — that is the right answer. (C) is correct: there are 4 parts in the Traffic Book — Part A (station accounts), Part B (net results of apportionment), Part C (Traffic Account — abstract of earnings and statement of balances), and Part D (adjustment balance sheet). Related fact: the final monthly adjustment traffic journal voucher is prepared on the basis of Part D. The principle behind this is worth grasping, not just memorising: once you understand why the rule is framed this way, the answer follows naturally instead of needing rote recall.

q: which earnings are not apportioned amongst railways?
e: luggage — that is the right answer. (B) is correct: luggage earnings are not apportioned among railways — they are retained by the collecting railway. Parcels, passengers and goods earnings are apportioned on distance basis among the railways carrying the traffic. Related fact: TTE earnings are likewise retained by the collecting railway. q: periodicity of apportionment of earnings amongst railways?
e: monthly — that is the right answer. (A) is correct: apportionment of earnings among railways is done monthly. Each month's through-traffic earnings are divided distance-wise among the participating railways. Related fact: the net results of this monthly apportionment appear in Part B of the Traffic Book. q: Traffic book part A deals with

q: The following instrument cant be accepted towards freight payment
e: (D) is correct: a cheque issued by a private party cannot be accepted towards freight payment — only demand drafts, e-payments, and cheques issued by PSUs are acceptable instruments. q: Cash acceptance limit for booking goods traffic
e: Option A (10 thousand) is the correct choice. q: For detaining privately owned wagons on railway lines beyond authorised free time what charges are collected?
e: Option D (Stabling) is the correct choice. (D) is correct: for detaining privately owned wagons on railway lines beyond the authorised free time, stabling charges are collected. Stabling is the charge for keeping private wagons standing on railway lines. Related fact: detention of railway wagons beyond free time attracts demurrage, while detention of consignments in railway premises attracts wharfage. Notice how precisely the correct option is worded. The paper tests exact scope here, not an approximate idea, which is why careful reading of the question stem matters.

q: PFT stands for
e: Private Freight Terminal — that is the right answer. PFT stands for Private Freight Terminal: a privately developed freight terminal notified under the Railway Board's PFT policy for handling rail traffic. The agreement period for a PFT is 30 years.

q: For detaining wagons beyond free time, what charges are collected?
e: (D) is correct: for detaining wagons beyond the permissible free time, demurrage charges are collected. Demurrage is the charge for holding railway wagons for loading/unloading beyond the allowed free time. Demurrage is the charge for detaining wagons beyond free time; wharfage is for occupying goods sheds/sidings beyond free time. q: For detaining inward consignments in railway premises what charges are collected?
e: The correct answer is wharfage. (A) is correct: for detaining inward consignments in railway premises (goods shed/platform) beyond free time, wharfage charges are collected. Wharfage is levied on the goods occupying railway premises, not on the wagon. Related fact: goods sheds are classified into Groups I, II and III based on the average number of rakes handled per month, which decides the wharfage free time. A useful way to verify this in the exam hall is to ask what would break if the opposite were true — the logic of the underlying system points straight to this option.
